questions.prompt: Which of these HTTP methods are idempotent? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — repeating them has the same effect as doing them once. POST is not idempotent.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that GET is a 'safe' method?

options.text: It is read-only and does not change server state

questions.explanation: A safe method is read-only. GET (and HEAD) retrieve data without changing server state.

questions.prompt: Why does a POST that charges a customer's card need an idempotency key?

options.text: POST is not idempotent, so a network retry could charge twice; the key lets the server recognize the retry

questions.explanation: Because POST is not idempotent, a retry could create a second charge. An idempotency key lets the server return the original result instead of acting again.

questions.prompt: Match each API style to what it is best suited for.

pairs.right: Rich clients fetching exactly the fields they need

questions.explanation: REST suits public resource CRUD, gRPC suits efficient internal RPC, and GraphQL lets clients request precisely the data they want.

questions.prompt: A client requests a user that does not exist. What should the API return?
questions.explanation: 404 Not Found precisely communicates that the resource doesn't exist. Returning 200 hides the failure and confuses clients, caches, and monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why is cursor (keyset) pagination usually better than offset pagination for very large, changing datasets?

options.text: It returns more results per page
It stays fast and stable as data grows and changes, while deep offsets get slow and shift
It does not require a database

questions.explanation: Deep offsets get slower the further you page and shift when items are inserted. A cursor points to where you left off, staying fast and stable.
